entries.be718fc9fc8b2beab317fddc4920bd25847767b8: <div sID="gen17750" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Jer.25" sID="Jer.25"/> <div eID="gen17750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17751" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17752" type="x-p"/> The prophecy of this chapter bears date some time before those prophecies in the chapters next foregoing, for they are not placed in the exact order of time in which they were delivered. This is dated in the first year of Nebuchadrezzar, that remarkable year when the sword of the Lord began to be drawn and furbished. Here is, I. A review of the prophecies that had been delivered to Judah and Jerusalem for many years past, by Jeremiah himself and other prophets, with the little regard given to them and the little success of them, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.1-Jer.25.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. A very express threatening of the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem, by the king of Babylon, for their contempt of God, and their continuance in sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.8-Jer.25.11">ver. 8-11</reference>), to which is annexed a promise of their deliverance out of their captivity in Babylon, after 70 years, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12-Jer.25.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. III. A prediction of the devastation of divers other nations about, by Nebuchadrezzar, represented by a "cup of fury" put into their hands (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.28">ver. 15-28</reference>), by a sword sent among them (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.29-Jer.25.33">ver. 29-33</reference>), and a desolation made among the shepherds and their flocks and pastures (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.34-Jer.25.38">ver. 34-38</reference>); so that we have here judgment beginning at the house of God, but not ending there.
entries.6273574af1118157015e55807265bec3b2145bb3: <div eID="gen17752" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17751" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Remonstrances with the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17753" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; <hi type="super">2</hi> The which Jeremiah the prophet spake unto all the people of Judah, and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, <hi type="super">3</hi> From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, even unto this day, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> the three and twentieth year, the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath come unto me, and I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye have not hearkened. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sent unto you all his servants the prophets, rising early and sending <hi type="italic">them;</hi> but ye have not hearkened, nor inclined your ear to hear. <hi type="super">5</hi> They said, Turn ye again now every one from his evil way, and from the evil of your doings, and dwell in the land that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath given unto you and to your fathers for ever and ever: <hi type="super">6</hi> And go not after other gods to serve them, and to worship them, and provoke me not to anger with the works of your hands; and I will do you no hurt. <hi type="super">7</hi> Yet ye have not hearkened unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; that ye might provoke me to anger with the works of your hands to your own hurt. <div eID="gen17753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17754" type="x-p"/> We have here a message from God concerning all the people of Judah (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.1">v. 1</reference>), which Jeremiah delivered, in his name, unto all the people of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, That which is of universal concern ought to be of universal cognizance. It is fit that the word which concerns all the people, as the word of God does, the word of the gospel particularly, should be divulged to all in general, and, as far as may be, addressed to each in particular. Jeremiah had been sent to the <hi type="italic">house of the king</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.1">ch. xxii. 1</reference>), and he took courage to deliver his message to them, probably when they had all come up to Jerusalem to worship at one of the solemn feasts; then he had them together, and it was to be hoped then, if ever, they would be well disposed to hear counsel and receive instruction. <div eID="gen17754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17755" type="x-p"/> This prophecy is dated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim and the first of Nebuchadrezzar. It was in the latter end of Jehoiakim's third year that Nebuchadrezzar began to reign by himself alone (having reigned some time before in conjunction with his father), as appears, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Dan. i. 1</reference>. But Jehoiakim's fourth year was begun before Nebuchadrezzar's first was completed. Now that that active, daring, martial prince began to set up for the world's master, God, by his prophet, gives notice that he is his servant, and intimates what work he intends to employ him in, that his growing greatness, which was so formidable to the nations, might not be construed as any reflection upon the power and providence of God in the government of the world. Nebuchadrezzar should not bid so fair for universal monarchy (I should have said universal tyranny) but that God had purposes of his own to serve by him, in the execution of which the world shall see the meaning of God's permitting and ordering a thing that seemed such a reflection on his sovereignty and goodness. <div eID="gen17755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17756" type="x-p"/> Now in this message we may observe the great pains that had been taken with the people to bring them to repentance, which they are here put in mind of, as an aggravation of their sin and a justification of God in his proceedings against them. <div eID="gen17756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17757" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah, for his part, had been a constant preacher among them twenty-three years; he began in the thirteenth year of Josiah, who reigned thirty-one years, so that he prophesied about eighteen or nineteen years in his reign, then in the reign of Jehoahaz, and now four years of Jehoiakim's reign. Note, God keeps an account, whether we do or no, how long we have enjoyed the means of grace; and the longer we have enjoyed them the heavier will our account be if we have not improved them. <hi type="italic">These three years</hi> (these three and twenty years) <hi type="italic">have I come seeking fruit on this fig-tree.</hi> All this while, 1. God had been constant in sending messages to them, as there was occasion for them: "From that time <hi type="italic">to this very day the word of the Lord has come into me,</hi> for your use." Though they had the substance of the warning sent them already in the books of Moses, yet, because those were not duly regarded and applied, God sent to enforce them and make them more particular, that they might be without excuse. Thus God's Spirit was striving with them, as with the old world, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>. 2. Jeremiah had been faithful and industrious in delivering those messages. He could appeal to themselves, as well as to God and his own conscience, concerning this: <hi type="italic">I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking.</hi> He had declared to them <hi type="italic">the whole counsel of God;</hi> he had taken a great deal of care and pains to discharge his thrust in such a manner as might be most likely to win and work upon them. What men are solicitous about and intent upon they rise up early to prosecute. It intimates that his head was so full of thoughts about it, and his heart so intent upon doing good, that it broke his sleep, and made him get up betimes to project which way he might take that would be most likely to do them good. He rose early, both because he would lose no time and because he would lay hold on and improve the best time to work upon them, when, if ever, they were sober and sedate. Christ came <hi type="italic">early in the morning</hi> to preach in the temple, and the people as early to hear him, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.38">Luke xxi. 38</reference>. Morning lectures have their advantages. <hi type="italic">My voice shalt thou hear in the morning.</hi> <div eID="gen17757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17758" type="x-p"/> II. Besides him, God had sent them other prophets, on the same errand, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.4">v. 4</reference>. Of the writing prophets Micah, Nahum, and Habakkuk, were a little before him, and Zephaniah contemporary with him. But, besides those, there were many other of God's <hi type="italic">servants the prophets</hi> who preached awakening sermons, which were never published. And here God himself is said to <hi type="italic">rise early</hi> and <hi type="italic">send them,</hi> intimating how much his heart also was upon it, that this people should <hi type="italic">turn and live,</hi> and not <hi type="italic">go on and die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.11">Ezek. xxxiii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen17758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17759" type="x-p"/> III. All the messages sent them were to the purpose, and much to the same purport, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.5-Jer.25.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. 1. They all told them of their faults, <hi type="italic">their evil way,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">evil of their doings.</hi> Those were not of God's sending who flattered them as if there were nothing amiss among them. 2. They all reproved them particularly for their idolatry, as a sin that was in a special manner provoking to God, their <hi type="italic">going after other gods, to serve them and to worship them,</hi> gods that were <hi type="italic">the work of their own hands.</hi> 3. They all called on them to repent of their sins and to reform their lives. This was the burden of every song, <hi type="italic">Turn you now every one from his evil way.</hi> Note, Personal and particular reformation must be insisted on as necessary to a national deliverance: <hi type="italic">every one</hi> must <hi type="italic">turn from his</hi> own <hi type="italic">evil way.</hi> The street will not be clean unless every one sweep before his own door. 4. They all assured them that, if they did so, it would certainly be the <hi type="italic">lengthening out of their tranquillity.</hi> The mercies they enjoyed should be continued to them: "<hi type="italic">You shall dwell in the land,</hi> dwell at ease, dwell in peace, in this good land, <hi type="italic">which the Lord has given you and your fathers.</hi> Nothing but sin will turn you out of it, and that shall not if you turn from it." The judgments they feared should be prevented: <hi type="italic">Provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt.</hi> Note, We should never receive from God the evil punishment if we did not provoke him by the evil of sin. God deals fairly with us, never corrects his children without cause, nor causes grief to us unless we give offence to him. <div eID="gen17759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17760" type="x-p"/> IV. Yet all was to no purpose. They were not wrought upon to take the right and only method to turn away the wrath of God. Jeremiah was a very lively affectionate preacher, yet <hi type="italic">they hearkened not</hi> to him, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.3">v. 3</reference>. The other prophets dealt faithfully with them, but neither did they <hi type="italic">hearken to them,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">incline their ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.4">v. 4</reference>. That very particular sin which they were told, of all others, was most offensive to God, and made them obnoxious to his justice, they wilfully persisted in: You <hi type="italic">provoke me with the works of your hands to your own hurt.</hi> Note, What is a provocation to God will prove, in the end, hurt to ourselves, and we must bear the blame of it. <hi type="italic">O Israel! thou hast destroyed thyself.</hi>
entries.cad0e3c650585c4002be7c2f6c8b7cd512476efd: <div eID="gen17760" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Desolation Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17761" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Because ye have not heard my words, <hi type="super">9</hi> Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and a hissing, and perpetual desolations. <hi type="super">10</hi> Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the candle. <hi type="super">11</hi> And this whole land shall be a desolation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. <hi type="super">12</hi> And it shall come to pass, when seventy years are accomplished, <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations. <hi type="super">13</hi> And I will bring upon that land all my words which I have pronounced against it, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah hath prophesied against all the nations. <hi type="super">14</hi> For many nations and great kings shall serve themselves of them also: and I will recompense them according to their deeds, and according to the works of their own hands. <div eID="gen17761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17762" type="x-p"/> Here is the sentence grounded upon the foregoing charge: "<hi type="italic">Because you have not heard my words,</hi> I must take another course with you," <reference osisRef="Jer.25.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, When men will not regard the judgments of God's mouth they may expect to feel the judgments of his hands, to hear the rod, since they would not hear the word; for the sinner must either be parted from his sin or perish in it. Wrath comes without remedy against those only that sin without repentance. It is not so much men's turning aside that ruins them as their not returning. <div eID="gen17762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17763" type="x-p"/> I. The ruin of the land of Judah by the king of Babylon's armies is here decreed, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9">v. 9</reference>. God sent to them <hi type="italic">his servants the prophets,</hi> and they were not heeded, and therefore God will send for <hi type="italic">his servant the king of Babylon,</hi> whom they cannot mock, and despise, and persecute, as they did his servants the prophets. Note, The messengers of God's wrath will be sent against those that would not receive the messengers of his mercy. One way or other God will be heeded, and will make men know that <hi type="italic">he is the Lord.</hi> Nebuchadrezzar, though a stranger to the true God, the God of Israel, nay, an enemy to him and afterwards a rival with him, was yet, in the descent he made upon his country. <hi type="italic">God's servant,</hi> accomplished his purpose, was employed by him, and was an instrument in his hand for the correction of his people. He was really serving God's designs when he thought he was serving his own ends. Justly therefore does God here call himself <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.8">v. 8</reference>), for here is an instance of his sovereign dominion, not only over the inhabitants, but over the armies of this earth, of which he makes what use he pleases. He has them all at his command. The most potent and absolute monarchs are his servants. Nebuchadrezzar, who is an instrument of his wrath, is as truly his servant as Cyrus, who is an instrument of his mercy. The land of Judah being to be made desolate, God here musters his army that is to make it so, gathers it together, takes <hi type="italic">all the families of the north,</hi> if there be occasion for them, leads them on as their commander-in-chief, <hi type="italic">brings them against this land,</hi> gives them success, not only against Judah and Jerusalem, but against <hi type="italic">all the nations round about,</hi> that there might be no dependence upon them as allies or assistants against that threatening force. The utter destruction of this and all the neighbouring lands is here described, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9-Jer.25.11">v. 9-11</reference>. It shall be total: <hi type="italic">The whole land shall be a desolation,</hi> not only desolate, but a desolation itself; both city and country shall be laid waste, and all the wealth of both be made a prey of. It shall be lasting, even <hi type="italic">perpetual desolations;</hi> they shall continue so long in ruins, and after long waiting there shall appear so little prospect of relief, that every one shall call it perpetual. This desolation shall be the ruin of their credit among their neighbours; it shall bury their honour in the dust, shall <hi type="italic">make them an astonishment and a hissing;</hi> every one will be amazed at them, and hiss them off the stage of action with just disgrace for deserting a God who would have been their protection for impostors who would certainly be their destruction. It will likewise be the ruin of all their comfort among themselves; it shall be a final period of all their joy: <hi type="italic">I will take from them the voice of mirth,</hi> hang their harps on the willow-trees, and put them out of tune for songs. <hi type="italic">I will take from them the voice of mirth;</hi> they shall neither have cause for it nor hearts for it. They would not hear the voice of God's word and therefore the voice of mirth shall no more be heard among them. They shall be deprived of food: <hi type="italic">The sound of the mill-stones shall not be heard;</hi> for, when the enemy has seized their stores, the sound of the grinding must needs be low, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.4">Eccl. xii. 4</reference>. An end shall be put to all business; there shall not be seen <hi type="italic">the light of a candle,</hi> for there shall be no work to be done worth candle-light. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> they shall be deprived of their liberty: <hi type="italic">Those nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.</hi> The fixing of time during which the captivity should last would be of great use, not only for the confirmation of the prophecy, when the event (which in this particular could by no human sagacity be foreseen) should exactly answer the prediction, but for the comfort of the people of God in their calamity and the encouragement of faith and prayer. Daniel, who was himself a prophet, had an eye to it, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Dan. ix. 2</reference>. Nay, God himself had an eye to it (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.22">2 Chron. xxxvi. 22</reference>); for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he <hi type="italic">stirred up the spirit of Cyrus,</hi> that the word spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished. <hi type="italic">Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world,</hi> which appears by this, that, when he has thought fit, some of them have been made known to his servants the prophets and by them to his church. <div eID="gen17763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17764" type="x-p"/> II. The ruin of Babylon, at last, is here likewise foretold, as it had been, long before, by Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12-Jer.25.14">v. 12-14</reference>. The destroyers must themselves be destroyed, and the rod thrown into the fire, when the correcting work is done with it. This shall be done when <hi type="italic">seventy years are accomplished;</hi> for the destruction of Babylon must make way for the deliverance of the captives. It is a great doubt when these <hi type="italic">seventy years</hi> commence; some date them from the captivity in the fourth year of Jehoiakim and first of Nebuchadrezzar, others from the captivity of Jehoiachin eight years after. I rather incline to the former, because then these nations began <hi type="italic">to serve the king of Babylon,</hi> and because usually God has taken the earliest time from which to reckon the accomplishment of a promise of mercy, as will appear in computing the 400 years' servitude in Egypt. And, if so, eighteen or nineteen years of the seventy had run out before Jerusalem and the temple were quite destroyed in the eleventh year of Zedekiah. However that be, when the time, the set time, to favour Zion, has come, the king of Babylon must be visited, and all the instances of his tyranny reckoned for; then that nation shall be punished <hi type="italic">for their iniquity,</hi> as the other nations have been punished for theirs. That land must then be a <hi type="italic">perpetual desolation,</hi> such as they had made other lands; for the <hi type="italic">Judge of all the earth</hi> will both <hi type="italic">do right</hi> and <hi type="italic">avenge wrong,</hi> as King of nations and King of saints. Let proud conquerors and oppressors be moderate in the use of their power and success, for it will come at last to their own turn to suffer; their day will come to fall. In this destruction of Babylon, which was to be brought about by the Medes and Persians, reference shall be had, 1. To what God had said: <hi type="italic">I will bring upon that land all my words;</hi> for all the wealth and honour of Babylon shall be sacrificed to the truth of the divine predictions, and all its power broken, rather than one iota or tittle of God's word shall fall to the ground. The same Jeremiah that prophesied the destruction of other nations by the Chaldeans foretold also the destruction of the Chaldeans themselves; and this must be brought upon them, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.13">v. 13</reference>. It is with reference to this very event that God says, I will <hi type="italic">confirm the word of my servant,</hi> and <hi type="italic">perform the counsel of my messengers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 26</reference>. 2. Two what they had done (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will recompense them according to their deeds,</hi> by which they transgressed the law of God, even then when they were made to serve his purposes. They had made many nations to serve them, and trampled upon them with the greatest insolence imaginable; but not that the measure of their iniquity is full <hi type="italic">many nations and great kings,</hi> that are in alliance with and come in to the assistance of Cyrus king of Persia, shall <hi type="italic">serve themselves of them</hi> also, shall make themselves masters of their country, enrich themselves with their spoils, and make them the footstool by which to mount the throne of universal monarchy. They shall make use of them for servants and soldiers. <hi type="italic">He that leads into captivity shall go into captivity.</hi>
entries.fe5defedb97abd8e8d80ce03ebc42fb32e5cd11f: <div eID="gen17764" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cup of Wrath; General Desolation. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17765" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they shall drink, and be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then took I the cup at the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's hand, and made all the nations to drink, unto whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had sent me: <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">To wit,</hi> Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and the kings thereof, and the princes thereof, to make them a desolation, an astonishment, a hissing, and a curse; as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> this day; <hi type="super">19</hi> Pharaoh king of Egypt, and his servants, and his princes, and all his people; <hi type="super">20</hi> And all the mingled people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, and all the kings of the land of the Philistines, and Ashkelon, and Azzah, and Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod, <hi type="super">21</hi> Edom, and Moab, and the children of Ammon, <hi type="super">22</hi> And all the kings of Tyrus, and all the kings of Zidon, and the kings of the isles which <hi type="italic">are</hi> beyond the sea, <hi type="super">23</hi> Dedan, and Tema, and Buz, and all <hi type="italic">that are</hi> in the utmost corners, <hi type="super">24</hi> And all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mingled people that dwell in the desert, <hi type="super">25</hi> And all the kings of Zimri, and all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of the Medes, <hi type="super">26</hi> And all the kings of the north, far and near, one with another, and all the kingdoms of the world, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the face of the earth: and the king of Sheshach shall drink after them. <hi type="super">27</hi> Therefore thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Drink ye, and be drunken, and spue, and fall, and rise no more, because of the sword which I will send among you. <hi type="super">28</hi> And it shall be, if they refuse to take the cup at thine hand to drink, then shalt thou say unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Ye shall certainly drink. <hi type="super">29</hi> For, lo, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should ye be utterly unpunished? Ye shall not be unpunished: for I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen17765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17766" type="x-p"/> Under the similitude of a cup going round, which all the company must drink of, is here represented the universal desolation that was now coming upon that part of the world which Nebuchadrezzar, who just now began to reign and act, was to be the instrument of, and which should at length recoil upon his own country. The cup in the vision is to be a sword in the accomplishment of it: so it is explained, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.16">v. 16</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the sword that I will send among them,</hi> the sword of war, that should be irresistibly strong and implacably cruel. <div eID="gen17766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17767" type="x-p"/> I. As to the circumstances of this judgment, observe, <div eID="gen17767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17768" type="x-p"/> 1. Whence this destroying sword should come—<hi type="italic">from the hand of God.</hi> It is the <hi type="italic">sword of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.47.6">ch. xlvii. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">bathed in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Isa. xxxiv. 5</reference>. Wicked men are made use of as his sword, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Ps. xvii. 13</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the wine-cup of his fury.</hi> It is the just anger of God that sends this judgment. The nations have provoked him by their sins, and they must fall under the tokens of his wrath. These are compared to some intoxicating liquor, which they shall be forced to drink of, as, formerly, condemned malefactors were sometimes executed by being compelled to drink poison. The wicked are said to <hi type="italic">drink the wrath of the Almighty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.20">Job xxi. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Rev. xiv. 10</reference>. Their share of troubles in his world is represented by the dregs of a cup of red wine full of mixture, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Ps. lxxv. 8</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Ps. xi. 6</reference>. The wrath of God in this world is but as a cup, in comparison of the full streams of it in the other world. <div eID="gen17768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17769" type="x-p"/> 2. By whose hand it should be sent to them—by the hand of Jeremiah as the judge <hi type="italic">set over the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">ch. i. 10</reference>), to pass his sentence upon them, and by the hand of Nebuchadrezzar as the executioner. What a much greater figure then does the poor prophet make than what the potent prince makes, if we look upon their relation to God, though in the eye of the world it was the reverse of it! Jeremiah must <hi type="italic">take the cup at God's hand,</hi> and compel the nations <hi type="italic">to drink it.</hi> He foretels no hurt to them but what God appoints him to foretel; and what is foretold by a divine authority will certainly be fulfilled by a divine power. <div eID="gen17769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17770" type="x-p"/> 3. On whom it should be sent—on all the nations within the verge of Israel's acquaintance and the lines of their communication. Jeremiah took the cup, and <hi type="italic">made all the nations to drink of it,</hi> that is, he prophesied concerning each of the nations here mentioned that they should share in this great desolation that was coming. <hi type="italic">Jerusalem and the cities of Judah</hi> are put first (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.18">v. 18</reference>); for <hi type="italic">judgment begins at the house of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1 Pet. iv. 17</reference>), at the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Ezek. ix. 6</reference>. Whether Nebuchadrezzar had his eye principally upon Jerusalem and Judah in this expedition or no does not appear; probably he had; for it was as considerable as any of the nations here mentioned. However God had his eye principally to them. And this part of the prophecy was already begun to be accomplished; this is denoted by that melancholy parenthesis (<hi type="italic">as it is this day</hi>), for in the fourth year of Jehoiakim things had come into a very bad posture, and all the foundations were out of course. <hi type="italic">Pharaoh king of Egypt</hi> comes next, because the Jews trusted to that broken reed (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.19">v. 19</reference>); the remains of them fled to Egypt, and there Jeremiah particularly foretold the destruction of that country, <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10-Jer.43.11">ch. xliii. 10, 11</reference>. All the other nations that bordered upon Canaan must pledge Jerusalem in this bitter cup, this cup of trembling. The <hi type="italic">mingled people,</hi> the Arabians (so some), some rovers of divers nations that lived by rapine (so others); <hi type="italic">the kings of the land of Uz,</hi> joined to the country of the Edomites. The Philistines had been vexatious to Israel, but now their cities and their lords become a prey to this mighty conqueror. Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Zidon, are places well known to border upon Israel; the <hi type="italic">Isles beyond,</hi> or <hi type="italic">beside, the sea,</hi> are supposed to be those parts of Phœnicia and Syria that lay upon the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. Dedan and the other countries mentioned (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.23-Jer.25.24">v. 23, 24</reference>) seem to have lain upon the confines of Idumea and Arabia the desert. Those of Elam are the Persians, with whom the Medes are joined, now looked upon as inconsiderable and yet afterwards able to make reprisals upon Babylon for themselves and all their neighbours. The <hi type="italic">kings of the north,</hi> that lay nearer to Babylon, and others that lay at some distance, will be sure to be seized on and made a prey of by the victorious sword of Nebuchadrezzar. Nay, he shall push on his victories with such incredible fury and success that all the kingdoms of the world that were then and there known should become sacrifices to his ambition. Thus Alexander is said to have conquered <hi type="italic">the world,</hi> and the Roman empire is called <hi type="italic">the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Luke ii. 1</reference>. Or it may be taken as reading the doom of <hi type="italic">all the kingdoms</hi> of the earth; one time or other, they shall feel the dreadful effects of war. The world has been, and will be, a great cockpit, while men's lusts war as they do <hi type="italic">in their members,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.4.1">Jam. iv. 1</reference>. But, that the conquerors may see their fate with the conquered, it concludes, <hi type="italic">The king of Sheshach shall drink after them,</hi> that is, the king of Babylon himself, who has given his neighbours all this trouble and vexation, shall at length have it return upon his own head. That by Sheshach is meant Babylon is plain from <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">ch. li. 41</reference>; but whether it was another name of the same city or the name of another city of the same kingdom is uncertain. Babylon's ruin was foretold, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12-Jer.25.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. Upon this prophecy of its being the author of the ruin of so many nations it is very fitly repeated here again. <div eID="gen17770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17771" type="x-p"/> 4. What should be the effect of it. The desolations which the sword should make in all these kingdoms are represented by the consequences of excessive drinking (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall drink, and be moved, and be mad. They shall be drunken, and spue, and fall and rise no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.27">v. 27</reference>. Now this may serve, (1.) To make us loathe the sin of drunkenness, that the consequences of it are made use of to set forth a most woeful and miserable condition. Drunkenness deprives men, for the present, of the use of their reason, makes them mad. It takes from them likewise that which, next to reason, is the most valuable blessing, and that is health; it makes them sick, and endangers the bones and the life. Men in drink often <hi type="italic">fall and rise no more;</hi> it is a sin that is its own punishment. How wretchedly are those intoxicated and besotted that suffer themselves at any time to be intoxicated, especially to be by the frequent commission of the sin besotted with wine or strong drink! (2.) To make us dread the judgments of war. When God sends the sword upon a nation, with warrant to make it desolate, it soon becomes like a drunken man, filled with confusion at the alarms of war, put into a hurry; its counsellors <hi type="italic">mad,</hi> and at their wits' end, staggering in all the measures they take, all the motions they make, sick at heart with continual vexation, <hi type="italic">vomiting up the riches</hi> they have greedily <hi type="italic">swallowed down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.15">Job xx. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">falling</hi> down before the enemy, and as unable to get up again, or do any thing to help themselves, as a man <hi type="italic">dead drunk is,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.16">Hab. ii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen17771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17772" type="x-p"/> 5. The undoubted certainty of it, with the reason given for it, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.28-Jer.25.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. They will <hi type="italic">refuse to take the cup at thy hand;</hi> not only they will be loth that the judgment should come, but they will be loth to believe that ever it will come; they will not give credit to the prediction of so despicable a man as Jeremiah. But he must tell them that it is <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord of hosts,</hi> he hath said it; and it is in vain for them to struggle with Omnipotence: <hi type="italic">You shall certainly drink.</hi> And he must give them this reason, It is a time of visitation, it is a reckoning day, and Jerusalem has been called to an account already: <hi type="italic">I begin to bring evil on the city that is called by my name;</hi> its relation to me will not exempt it from punishment, and <hi type="italic">should you be utterly unpunished?</hi> No; <hi type="italic">If this be done in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?</hi> If those who have some good in them smart so severely for the evil that is found in them, can those expect to escape who have worse evils, and no good, found among them? If Jerusalem be punished for learning idolatry of the nations, shall not the nations be punished, of whom they learned it? No doubt they shall: <hi type="italic">I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth,</hi> for they have helped to debauch the inhabitants of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen17772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17773" type="x-p"/> II. Upon this whole matter we may observe, 1. That there is a God that judges in the earth, to whom all the nations of the earth are accountable, and by whose judgment they must abide. 2. That God can easily bring to ruin the greatest nations, the most numerous and powerful, and such as have been most secure. 3. That those who have been vexatious and mischievous to the people of God will be reckoned with for it at last. Many of these nations had in their turns given disturbance to Israel, but now comes destruction on them. The year of the redeemer will come, even the <hi type="italic">year of recompenses</hi> for the controversy of Zion. 4. That the <hi type="italic">burden of the word of the Lord</hi> will at last become the burden of his judgments. Isaiah had prophesied long since against most of these nations (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.27">ch. xiii.</reference>, &c.) and now at length all his prophecies will have their complete fulfilling. 5. That those who are ambitious of power and dominion commonly become the troublers of the earth and the plagues of their generation. Nebuchadrezzar was so proud of his might that he had no sense of right. These are the men that turn the world upside down, and yet expect to be admired and adored. Alexander thought himself a great prince when others thought him no better than a great pirate. 6. That the greatest pomp and power in this world are of very uncertain continuance. Before Nebuchadrezzar's greater force kings themselves must yield and become captives.
entries.1a9bf4116e6ad685472a58e715869d054723bf1a: <div eID="gen17773" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">General Desolation; Jeremiah's Faithful Preaching. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17774" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> Therefore prophesy thou against them all these words, and say unto them, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation; he shall mightily roar upon his habitation; he shall give a shout, as they that tread <hi type="italic">the grapes,</hi> against all the inhabitants of the earth. <hi type="super">31</hi> A noise shall come <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the ends of the earth; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath a controversy with the nations, he will plead with all flesh; he will give them <hi type="italic">that are</hi> wicked to the sword, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">32</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, Behold, evil shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind shall be raised up from the coasts of the earth. <hi type="super">33</hi> And the slain of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be at that day from <hi type="italic">one</hi> end of the earth even unto the <hi type="italic">other</hi> end of the earth: they shall not be lamented, neither gathered, nor buried; they shall be dung upon the ground. <hi type="super">34</hi> Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves <hi type="italic">in the ashes,</hi> ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the shepherds shall have no way to flee, nor the principal of the flock to escape. <hi type="super">36</hi> A voice of the cry of the shepherds, and a howling of the principal of the flock, <hi type="italic">shall be heard:</hi> for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoiled their pasture. <hi type="super">37</hi> And the peaceable habitations are cut down because of the fierce anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">38</hi> He hath forsaken his covert, as the lion: for their land is desolate because of the fierceness of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger. <div eID="gen17774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17775" type="x-p"/> We have, in these verses, a further description of those terrible desolations which the king of Babylon with his armies should make in all the countries and nations round about Jerusalem. In Jerusalem God had erected his temple; there were his oracles and ordinances, which the neighbouring nations should have attended to and might have received benefit by; thither they should have applied for the knowledge of God and their duty, and then they might have had reason to bless God for their neighbourhood to Jerusalem; but they, instead of that, taking all opportunities either to debauch or to disturb that holy city, when God came to reckon with Jerusalem because it learned so much of the <hi type="italic">way of the nations,</hi> he reckoned with the nations because they learned so little of the way of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen17775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17776" type="x-p"/> They will soon be aware of Nebuchadrezzar's making war upon them; but the prophet is here directed to tell them that it is God himself that makes war upon them, a God with whom there is no contending. 1. The war is here proclaimed (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord shall roar from on high;</hi> not <hi type="italic">from Mount Zion and Jerusalem</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">Joel iii. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">Amos i. 2</reference>), but from <hi type="italic">heaven,</hi> from <hi type="italic">his holy habitation</hi> there; for now Jerusalem is one of the places against which he roars. <hi type="italic">He shall mightily roar upon his habitation</hi> on earth from that above. He has been long silent, and seemed not to take notice of the wickedness of the nations; the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now <hi type="italic">he shall give a shout,</hi> as the assailants in battle do, <hi type="italic">against all the inhabitants of the earth,</hi> to whom it shall be a shout of terror, and yet a shout of joy in heaven, as theirs that <hi type="italic">tread the grapes;</hi> for, when God is reckoning with the proud enemies of his kingdom among men, there is a <hi type="italic">great voice of much people heard in heaven, saying, Hallelujah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1">Rev. xix. 1</reference>. He <hi type="italic">roars as a lion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Amos iii. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">8</reference>), as a lion that has <hi type="italic">forsaken his covert</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.38">v. 38</reference>), and is going abroad to seek his prey, upon which he roars, that he may the more easily seize it. 2. The manifesto is here published, showing the causes and reasons why God proclaims this war (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has a controversy with the nations;</hi> he has just cause to contend with them, and he will take this way of pleading with them. His quarrel with them is, in one word, for their wickedness, their contempt of him, and his authority over them and kindness to them. <hi type="italic">He will give those that are wicked to the sword.</hi> They have provoked God to anger, and thence comes all this destruction; it is <hi type="italic">because of the fierce anger of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.37-Jer.25.38">v. 37 and again v. 38</reference>), the <hi type="italic">fierceness of the oppressor,</hi> or (as it might better be read) <hi type="italic">the fierceness of the oppressing sword</hi> (for the word is feminine) is <hi type="italic">because of his fierce anger;</hi> and we are sure that he is never angry without cause; but <hi type="italic">who knows the power of his anger?</hi> 3. The alarm is here given and taken: <hi type="italic">A noise will come even to the ends of the earth,</hi> so loud shall it roar, so far shall it reach, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.31">v. 31</reference>. The alarm is not given by sound of trumpet, or beat of drum, but by a <hi type="italic">whirlwind, a great whirlwind, storm,</hi> or <hi type="italic">tempest,</hi> which shall be <hi type="italic">raised up from the coasts,</hi> the remote coasts <hi type="italic">of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.32">v. 32</reference>. The Chaldean army shall be like a hurricane raised in the north, but thence carried on with incredible fierceness and swiftness, bearing down all before it. It is like the whirlwind out of which God answered Job, which was exceedingly terrible, <reference osisRef="Job.37.1">Job xxxvii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.1">xxxviii. 1</reference>. And, when the wrath of God thus roars like a lion from heaven, no marvel if it be echoed with shrieks from earth; for who can choose but tremble when God thus speaks in displeasure? See <reference osisRef="Hos.11.10">Hosea xi. 10</reference>. Now the shepherds shall <hi type="italic">howl and cry,</hi> the kings, and princes, and the great ones of the earth, the <hi type="italic">principal of the flock.</hi> They used to be the most courageous and secure, but now their hearts shall fail them; <hi type="italic">they shall wallow themselves in the ashes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.34">v. 34</reference>. Seeing themselves utterly unable to make head against the enemy, and seeing their country, which they have the charge of and a concern for, inevitably ruined, they shall abandon themselves to sorrow. There shall be <hi type="italic">a voice of the cry of the shepherds,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">howling of the principal of the flock shall be heard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.36">v. 36</reference>. Those are great calamities indeed that strike such a terror upon the great men, and put them into this consternation. <hi type="italic">The Lord hath spoiled their pasture,</hi> in which they fed their flock, and out of which they fed themselves; the spoiling of that makes them cry-out thus. Perhaps, carrying on the metaphor of a lion roaring, it alludes to the great fright that shepherds are in when they hear a roaring lion coming towards their flocks, and find they have <hi type="italic">no way to flee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.35">v. 35</reference>) for their own safety, neither can the <hi type="italic">principal of their flock escape.</hi> The enemy will be so numerous, so furious, so sedulous, and the extent of their armies so vast, that it will be impossible to avoid falling into their hands. Note, As we cannot out-face, so we cannot out-run, the judgments of God. This is that for which the shepherds <hi type="italic">howl and cry.</hi> 4. The progress of this war is here described (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, evil shall go forth from nation to nation;</hi> as the cup goes round, every nation shall have its share and take warning by the calamities of another to repent and reform. Nay, as if this ere to be a little representation of the last and general judgment, it shall reach <hi type="italic">from one end of the earth even unto the other end of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.33">v. 33</reference>. The day of vengeance is in his heart, and now <hi type="italic">his hand shall find out all his enemies,</hi> wherever they are, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.8">Ps. xxi. 8</reference>. Note, When our neighbour's house is on fire it is time to be concerned for our own. When one nation is a seat of war every neighbouring nation should hear, and fear, and make its peace with God. 5. The dismal consequences of this war are here foretold: <hi type="italic">The days of slaughter and dispersions are accomplished,</hi> that is, they are fully come (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.34">v. 34</reference>), the time fixed in the divine counsel for the slaughter of some and the dispersion of the rest, which will make the nations completely desolate. Multitudes shall fall by the sword of the merciless Chaldeans, so that <hi type="italic">the slain of the Lord</hi> shall be every where found: they are slain by commission from him, and are sacrificed to his justice. The slain for sin are the <hi type="italic">slain of the Lord.</hi> To complete the misery of their slaughter, <hi type="italic">they shall not be lamented</hi> in particular, so general shall the matter of lamentation be. Nay, they shall not <hi type="italic">be gathered</hi> up, nor <hi type="italic">buried,</hi> for they shall have no friends left to bury them, and the enemies shall not have so much humanity in them as to do it; and then they shall be <hi type="italic">as dung upon the earth,</hi> so vile and noisome: and it is well if, as dung manures the earth and makes it fruitful, so these horrid spectacles, which lie as monuments of divine justice, might be a means to awaken the inhabitants of the earth to <hi type="italic">learn righteousness.</hi> The effect of this war will be the <hi type="italic">desolation of the whole land</hi> that is the seat of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.38">v. 38</reference>), one land after another. But here are two expressions more that seem to make the case in a particular manner piteous. (1.) <hi type="italic">You shall fall like a pleasant vessel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.34">v. 34</reference>. The most desirable persons among them, who most valued themselves and were most valued, who were looked upon as <hi type="italic">vessels of honour,</hi> shall fall by the sword. You shall fall as a Venice glass or a China dish, which is soon broken all to pieces. Even the tender and delicate shall share in the common calamity; the sword devours one as well as another. (2.) Even <hi type="italic">the peaceable habitations are cut down.</hi> Those that used to be quiet, and not molested, the habitations in which you have long dwelt in peace, shall now be no longer such, but <hi type="italic">cut down</hi> by the war. Or, Those who used to be quiet, and not molesting any of their neighbours, those who lived in peace, easily, and gave no provocation to any, even those shall not escape. This is one of the direful effects of war, that even those who were most harmless and inoffensive suffer hard things. Blessed be God, there is a <hi type="italic">peaceable habitation</hi> above for all the sons of peace, which is out of the reach of fire and sword.  <chapter eID="Jer.25"/> <div eID="gen17776" type="x-p"/>

entries.457c58fb7e8f1b488de6609a0b63d1031e89a80e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10121"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.25.1-Jer.25.38">Jr 25:1-38</reference>. Prophecy of the Seventy Years' Captivity; and after That the Destruction of Babylon, and of All the Nations That Oppressed the Jews.</title> <div sID="gen18051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10121"/><hi type="bold">1. fourth year of Jehoiakim--</hi>called the third year in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Da 1:1</reference>. But probably Jehoiakim was set on the throne by Pharaoh-necho on his return from Carchemish about July, whereas Nebuchadnezzar mounted the throne January 21, 604 B.C.; so that Nebuchadnezzar's first year was partly the third, partly the fourth, of Jehoiakim's. Here first Jeremiah gives specific dates. Nebuchadnezzar had previously entered Judea in the reign of his father Nabopolassar. <div eID="gen18051" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ba936eb9fe12690fbe68e99751d00c2b1404a02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10122"/><div sID="gen18052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10122"/>3. From the thirteenth year of Josiah, in which Jeremiah began to prophesy (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.1">Jr 1:1</reference>), to the end of Josiah's reign, was nineteen years (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.1">2Ki 22:1</reference>); the three months 2 Kings 23. 31) of Jehoahaz' reign, with the not quite complete four years of Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.1">Jr 25:1</reference>), added to the nineteen years, make up twenty-three years in all. <div eID="gen18052" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0595f86373e3a2f800969be5ea812b9ecf72b01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10123"/><div sID="gen18053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10123"/><hi type="bold">4. rising early--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.7.13">Jr 7:13</reference>). "The prophets" refer to Urijah, Zephaniah, Habakkuk, &c. It aggravates their sin, that God sent not merely one but many messengers, and those messengers, prophets; and, that during all those years specified, Jeremiah and his fellow prophets spared no effort, late and early. <div eID="gen18053" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d20178dbfd2bd6e51ed275be4e4ba544dad955a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10124"/><div sID="gen18054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10124"/><hi type="bold">5. Turn ... dwell--</hi>In Hebrew there is expressed by sameness of sounds the correspondence between their turning to God and God's turning to them to permit them to dwell in their land: Shubu ... shebu, "Return" ... so shall ye "remain."<div eID="gen18054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every one from ... evil--</hi>Each must separately repent and turn from his own sin. None is excepted, lest they should think their guilt extenuated because the evil is general. <div eID="gen18055" type="x-p"/>
entries.97267be56de6b7775e3a59bede79788542903e60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10125"/><div sID="gen18056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10125"/>6. He instances one sin, idolatry, as representative of all their sins; as nothing is dearer to God than a pure worship of Himself. <div eID="gen18056" type="x-p"/>
entries.30f175790355d226e915bea6ca16ec23c3614048: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10126"/><div sID="gen18057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10126"/>7. Though ye provoke Me to anger (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">De 32:21</reference>), yet it is not I, but yourselves, whom ye thereby hurt (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Pr 8:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.2">20:2</reference>). <div eID="gen18057" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa26b5760825aed8cb43d80900629fed0eaa45d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10127"/><div sID="gen18058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10127"/><hi type="bold">9. the north--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Jer.1.14">Jr 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>). The Medes and other northern peoples, confederate with Babylon, are included with the Chaldeans.<div eID="gen18058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my servant--</hi>My agent for punishing (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.6">Jr 27:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10">43:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.40.2">Jr 40:2</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Is 44:28</reference>; Cyrus, "My shepherd." God makes even unbelievers unconsciously to fulfil His designs. A reproof to the Jews, who boasted that they were the servants of God; yet a heathen king is to be more the servant of God than they, and that as the agent of their punishment. <div eID="gen18059" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7c108a773bd3f71314872aa47a418d2c0056f51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10128"/><div sID="gen18060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10128"/>10. (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">Jr 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.23">Re 18:23</reference>). The land shall be so desolated that even in the houses left standing there shall be no inhabitant; a terrible stillness shall prevail; no sound of the hand-mill (two circular stones, one above the other, for grinding corn, worked by two women, <reference osisRef="Exod.11.5">Ex 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.41">Mt 24:41</reference>; in daily use in every house, and therefore forbidden to be taken in pledge, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.6">De 24:6</reference>); no night-light, so universal in the East that the poorest house has it, burning all night.<div eID="gen18060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">candle--</hi>lamp (<reference osisRef="Job.21.17">Job 21:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.6">18:6</reference>). <div eID="gen18061" type="x-p"/>
entries.79cbf6432f72024f4c097255ee724f3335658bb5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10129"/><div sID="gen18062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10129"/><hi type="bold">11. seventy years--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jr 27:7</reference>). The exact number of years of Sabbaths in four hundred ninety years, the period from Saul to the Babylonian captivity; righteous retribution for their violation of the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.34">Le 26:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.21">2Ch 36:21</reference>). The seventy years probably begin from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Jerusalem was first captured, and many captives, as well as the treasures of the temple, were carried away; they end with the first year of Cyrus, who, on taking Babylon, issued an edict for the restoration of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1">Ezr 1:1</reference>). Daniel's seventy prophetic weeks are based on the seventy years of the captivity (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Da 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen18062" type="x-p"/>
entries.743048f6d1d44bdfa4f6f5bddf511791b894ffa9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10130"/><div sID="gen18063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10130"/><hi type="bold">13. all ... written in this book, which Jeremiah ... prophesied against all ... nations--</hi>It follows from this, that the prophecies against foreign nations (forty-sixth through fifty-first chapters) must have been already written. Hence the Septuagint inserts here those prophecies. But if they had followed immediately (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.13">Jr 25:13</reference>), there would have been no propriety in the observation in the verse. The very wording of the reference shows that they existed in some other part of the book, and not in the immediate context. It was in this very year, the fourth of Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.1">Jr 36:1</reference>, 2), that Jeremiah was directed to write in a regular book for the first time all that he had prophesied against Judah and foreign "nations" from the beginning of his ministry. Probably, at a subsequent time, when he completed the whole work, including the forty-sixth through fifty-first chapters, Jeremiah himself inserted the clause, "all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah hath prophesied against all the nations." The prophecies in question may have been repeated, as others in Jeremiah, more than once; so in the original smaller collection they may have stood in an earlier position; and, in the fuller subsequent collection, in their later and present position. <div eID="gen18063" type="x-p"/>
entries.64fab549f3156586c7c0a6bf29192b6f6669ac94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10131"/><div sID="gen18064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10131"/><hi type="bold">14. serve themselves--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jr 27:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.8">30:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.10">34:10</reference>). Avail themselves of their services as slaves.<div eID="gen18064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them also--</hi>the Chaldees, who heretofore have made other nations their slaves, shall themselves also in their turn be slaves to them. Maurer translates, "shall impose servitude on them, even them."<div eID="gen18065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">recompense them--</hi>namely, the Chaldees and other nations against whom Jeremiah had prophesied (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.13">Jr 25:13</reference>), as having oppressed the Jews.<div eID="gen18066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their deeds--</hi>rather, "deed," namely, their bad treatment of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jr 50:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">51:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.24">24</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.17">2Ch 36:17</reference>). <div eID="gen18067" type="x-p"/>
entries.4525eefc90e26ea2cc0f59e96e747f039fd97fd6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10132"/><div sID="gen18068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10132"/><hi type="bold">15. wine cup--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.13.12">Jr 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">13</reference>, as to this image, to express stupefying judgments; also <reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">Jr 49:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.7">51:7</reference>. Jeremiah often embodies the imagery of Isaiah in his prophecies (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17-Isa.51.22">Is 51:17-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.19">Re 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">18:6</reference>). The wine cup was not literally given by Jeremiah to the representatives of the different nations; but only in symbolical vision. <div eID="gen18068" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9ade6927e9f9730727c2f1859dad137f55c2a04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10133"/><div sID="gen18069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10133"/><hi type="bold">16. be moved--</hi>reel (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.11">Na 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18069" type="x-p"/>
entries.57302f344611e070a4220595cdc22c124f29aedd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10134"/><div sID="gen18070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10134"/><hi type="bold">18. Jerusalem--</hi>put first: for "judgment begins at the house of God"; they being most guilty whose religious privileges are greatest (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>).<div eID="gen18070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kings--</hi>Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah.<div eID="gen18071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it is this day--</hi>The accomplishment of the curse had already begun under Jehoiakim. This clause, however, may have been inserted by Jeremiah at his final revision of his prophecies in Egypt. <div eID="gen18072" type="x-p"/>
entries.4929448d107343873ea95289f046a574a2fc7fdf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10135"/><div sID="gen18073" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10135"/><hi type="bold">19. Pharaoh--</hi>put next after Jerusalem, because the Jews had relied most on him, and Egypt and Judea stood on a common footing (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.25">25</reference>). <div eID="gen18073" type="x-p"/>
entries.6859ec2a3ea09878225e830386a0c81ec20092f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10136"/><div sID="gen18074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10136"/><hi type="bold">20. mingled people--</hi>mercenary foreign troops serving under Pharaoh-hophra in the time of Jeremiah. The employment of these foreigners provoked the native Egyptians to overthrow him. Psammetichus, father of Pharaoh-necho, also had given a settlement in Egypt to Ionian and Carian adventurers [Herodotus, 2.152, 154]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">Jr 50:37</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Is 19:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1">Is 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>. The term is first found in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.38">Ex 12:38</reference>.<div eID="gen18074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Uz--</hi>in the geographical order here, between Egypt and the states along the Mediterranean; therefore not the "Uz" of <reference osisRef="Job.1.1">Job 1:1</reference> (north of Arabia-Deserta), but the northern part of Arabia-Petræa, between the sea and Idumea (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Gen.36.20">Ge 36:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.28">28</reference>).<div eID="gen18075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remnant of Ashdod--</hi>called a "remnant," because Ashdod had lost most of its inhabitants in the twenty-nine years siege by Psammetichus. Compare also see on <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1">Is 20:1</reference>. Gath is not mentioned because it was overthrown in the same war. <div eID="gen18076" type="x-p"/>
entries.babc3a963e8ede6a5cbc9bcd493b2b2221eb3fb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10137"/><div sID="gen18077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10137"/><hi type="bold">21. Edom ... Moab ... Ammon--</hi>joined together, as being related to Israel (see <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1-Jer.49.39">Jr 48:1-49:39</reference>). <div eID="gen18077" type="x-p"/>
entries.37f7a5c0bc498dbdadec6af4ff3a1b4c895d53e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10138"/><div sID="gen18078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10138"/><hi type="bold">22. all the kings of Tyrus--</hi>the petty kings of the various dependencies of Tyre.<div eID="gen18078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">isles--</hi>a term including all maritime regions (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">Psa 72:10</reference>). <div eID="gen18079" type="x-p"/>
entries.142b9f610b4cdb98b1f3438df51d61e078683783: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10139"/><div sID="gen18080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10139"/><hi type="bold">23. Dedan--</hi>north of Arabia (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Ge 25:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen18080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tema ... Buz--</hi>neighboring tribes north of Arabia (<reference osisRef="Job.32.2">Job 32:2</reference>).<div eID="gen18081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... in ... utmost corners--</hi>rather, "having the hair cut in angles," a heathenish custom (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.9.26">Jr 9:26</reference>). <div eID="gen18082" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac757313279c20d4557fe459c849cebd81999092: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10140"/><div sID="gen18083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10140"/><hi type="bold">24. mingled people--</hi>not in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Jer.25.20">Jr 25:20</reference>; the "motley crowd," so called in contempt (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.49.28">Jr 49:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">50:37</reference>). By a different pointing it may be translated the "Arabs"; but the repetition of the name is not likely. Blaney thinks there were two divisions of what we call Arabia, the west (Araba) and the east. The west included Arabia-Petræa and the parts on the sea bordering on Egypt, the land of Cush; the east, Arabia-Felix and Deserta. The latter are "the mixed race" inhabiting the desert. <div eID="gen18083" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba0ac8785cfffe03a94b05e97268d2cdd31d5f8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10141"/><div sID="gen18084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10141"/><hi type="bold">25. Zimri--</hi>perhaps the Zabra mentioned by Ptolemy between Mecca and Medina. Zimran also, as Dedan, was one of Abraham's sons by Keturah (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.2">Ge 25:2</reference>).<div eID="gen18084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Elam--</hi>properly, west of Persia; but used for Persia in general. <div eID="gen18085" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d42a312da15e2d3ce779ed162e6952ddb5de2a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10142"/><div sID="gen18086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10142"/><hi type="bold">26. Sheshach--</hi>Babylon; as the parallelism in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jr 51:41</reference> proves. In the Cabalistic system (called Athbash, the first Hebrew letter in the alphabet being expressed by the last) Sheshach would exactly answer to Babel. Jeremiah may have used this system (as perhaps in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jr 51:41</reference>) for concealment at the time of this prediction, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, while Nebuchadnezzar was before Jerusalem. In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jr 51:41</reference> there can be no concealment, as Babylon is expressly mentioned. Michaelis more simply explains the term "brazen-gated" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.2">Is 45:2</reference>); others, "the house of a prince." Rather, it comes from the Babylonian goddess, Shach, by reduplication of the first letter; from her Misael was named Meshach by the Babylonians. The term Shace was applied to a festival at Babylon, alluded to in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jr 51:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.57">57</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.5">Is 21:5</reference>. It was during this feast that Cyrus took Babylon [Herodotus, 1]. Thus Jeremiah mystically denotes the time of its capture by this term [Glassius]. <div eID="gen18086" type="x-p"/>
entries.66511727057b661bd4959e650dd5da395a6cf1df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10143"/><div sID="gen18087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10143"/><hi type="bold">27. rise no more--</hi>The heathen nations in question should fall to rise no more. The Jews should fall but for a time, and then rise again. Therefore, the epithet is given, "the God of Israel." <div eID="gen18087" type="x-p"/>
entries.15e75b06c98c476afb2b1d56d90e0c54f81d66d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10144"/><div sID="gen18088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10144"/><hi type="bold">28. if they refuse to take the cup--</hi>No effort of theirs to escape destruction will avail. <div eID="gen18088" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f80018f8ec6d3715832b0ed9a6a61f921a324b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10145"/><div sID="gen18089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10145"/>29. If I spared not Mine elect people on account of sin, much less will I spare you (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Eze 9:6</reference>; Ob 16; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.31">Lu 23:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>).<div eID="gen18089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be unpunished--</hi>"be treated as innocent." <div eID="gen18090" type="x-p"/>
entries.61b9034374cf38668c278eae6be0fdc7fe69720d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10146"/><div sID="gen18091" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10146"/><hi type="bold">30. roar--</hi>image from a destructive lion (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.13">Is 42:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">Joe 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen18091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon his habitation--</hi>rather, "His pasturage"; keeping up the image of a lion roaring against the flock in the pasture. The roar was first to go forth over Judea wherein were "the sheep of His pasture" (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>), and thence into heathen lands.<div eID="gen18092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shout ... tread ... grapes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.48.33">Jr 48:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Is 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen18093" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7d15f40acc4a2eb0436241fb3bbcc881f05cc09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10147"/><div sID="gen18094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10147"/><hi type="bold">31. controversy--</hi>cause at issue (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.2">Mi 6:2</reference>).<div eID="gen18094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plead with all flesh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Is 66:16</reference>). God shows the whole world that He does what is altogether just in punishing. <div eID="gen18095" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2478c31b5b9de7ab4096196a176a461841d77b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10148"/><div sID="gen18096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10148"/><hi type="bold">32. from the coasts--</hi>rather, "from the uttermost regions." Like a storm which arises in one region and then diffuses itself far and wide, so God's judgments shall pass "from nation to nation," till all has been fulfilled; no distance shall prevent the fulfilment.<div eID="gen18096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not be lamented--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.16.4">Jr 16:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen18097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither gathered--</hi>to their fathers, in their ancestral tombs (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">Jr 8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen18098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dung--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.83.10">Psa 83:10</reference>). <div eID="gen18099" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfc13a3a3eac45c9a9b01c2cbf217ebc95d0d2af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10149"/><div sID="gen18100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10149"/><hi type="bold">34. shepherds--</hi>princes (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.22">Jr 22:22</reference>). Here he returns to the Jews and their rulers, using the same image as in <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jr 25:30</reference>, "pasture" (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jr 25:30</reference>).<div eID="gen18100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wallow yourselves--</hi>Cover yourselves as thickly with ashes, in token of sorrow, as one who rolls in them (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.26">Jr 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.30">Eze 27:30</reference>) [Maurer].<div eID="gen18101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">principal--</hi>leaders. The Septuagint translates "rams," carrying out the image (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zec 10:3</reference>).<div eID="gen18102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">days of your slaughter ... of ... dispersions--</hi>rather, "your days for slaughter (that is, the time of your being slain), and your dispersions (not 'of your dispersions'), are accomplished (are come)."<div eID="gen18103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasant vessel--</hi>Ye were once a precious vessel, but ye shall fall, and so be a broken vessel (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">Jr 22:28</reference>). "Your past excellency shall not render you safe now. I will turn to your ignominy whatever glory I conferred on you" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18104" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3b81e480c93f5546c3468c4d73ce22c48c14945: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10150"/><div sID="gen18105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10150"/>35. Literally, "Flight shall fail the shepherds ... escaping (shall fail) the principal," &c. (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.14">Am 2:14</reference>). The leaders will be the first objects for slaughter; escape by flight will be out of their power. <div eID="gen18105" type="x-p"/>
entries.8039a659713765c3ed2a126bbe16443cd7b42f7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10151"/><div sID="gen18106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10151"/><hi type="bold">37. habitations--</hi>rather, carrying out the image "pastures" (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jr 25:30</reference>). The pasturages where, peaceably and without incursion of wild beasts, the flocks have fed, shall be destroyed; that is, the regions where, heretofore, there was peace and security (alluding to the name Salem, or Jerusalem, "possessing peace"). <div eID="gen18106" type="x-p"/>
entries.f812f94bb2ffd15b2cffed9c28cb2d6158ed2fb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10152"/><div sID="gen18107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10152"/><hi type="bold">38. his covert--</hi>the temple, where heretofore, like a lion, as its defender, by the mere terror of His voice He warded off the foe; but now He leaves it a prey to the Gentiles [Calvin].<div eID="gen18107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fierceness of ... oppressor--</hi>rather, as the Hebrew, for "oppressor" is an adjective feminine, the word "sword" is understood, which, in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.16">Jr 46:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.16">50:16</reference>, is expressed (indeed, some manuscripts and the Septuagint read "sword" instead of "fierceness" here; probably interpolated from <reference osisRef="Jer.46.16">Jr 46:16</reference>), "the oppressing sword." The Hebrew for "oppressing" means also a "dove": there may be, therefore, a covert allusion to the Chaldean standard bearing a dove on it, in honor of Semiramis, the first queen, said in popular superstition to have been nourished by doves when exposed at birth, and at death to have been transformed into a dove. Her name may come from a root referring to the cooing of a dove. That bird was held sacred to the goddess Venus. Vulgate so translates "the anger of the dove."<div eID="gen18108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his ... anger--</hi>If the anger of Nebuchadnezzar cannot be evaded, how much less that of God (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.25.37">Jr 25:37</reference>)! <chapter eID="Jer.25"/>

entries.2a9f164711010a940fbd919a6aa956ae81252b48: <div eID="gen29949" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29950" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29951" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29951" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29950" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29952" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains a summary of the judgments denounced by Jeremiah against Judah, Babylon, and many other nations.
